the inducible system of mutagenesis is not the sole mechanism of mutation fixation in UV-irradiated bacteria, and the existence of an alternative mechanism is indicated.
the inducible SOS mutagenesis system in E. coli is not the only one that can lead to the fixation of mutations in the absence of photoreactivation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fraction of mutations which are resistant to photorepair and to excision repair increases in the course of the normal process of mutagenesis, but this increase is not a direct consequence of the induction of mutagenesis.

the fraction of nonrepaired mutations in UV-irradiated E. coli cells is determined by the balance of two opposing mechanisms: one of them is the inducible system of mutagenesis and another one is a still unknown system of mutation repair.
the inducible and constitutive mutagenic systems are involved in the process of mutation fixation, but the latter one can be active only when cells are able to produce proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the process of mutation fixation in E. coli cells is more complex than previously thought and involves the participation of additional, as yet unknown mechanisms.
the induction of mutagenesis is a multistep process that involves both the inducible and the constitutive mutagenic systems.
the process of mutation fixation can be separated from the process of mutation induction.
